Glossary

    Figures in the plane

    Words: 2929

    A few axioms from which logic derives everything else. Geometry is the first place where mathematics appears not as a set of formulas but as a system: every property is proved from the previous ones.

    Main idea of the page #

    The angle sum of a triangle, the properties of a parallelogram, the inscribed angle are not separate facts but a chain: each is proved from the previous ones, and at the base lies the axiom of parallel lines. So in geometry one rule holds: «it looks equal on the figure» is no argument. The block can establish shape and equality; measuring lengths and areas is the task of the next block (11).

    Step 0 · Hook

    1 · Is an inscribed angle equal to the central one? #

    A central angle of a circle is 80°. What is the inscribed angle that stands on the same arc? The habit «they stand on one arc, so they are equal» gives 80°. In fact the inscribed angle is half as large: 40°. Both angles «look» at one arc, but from different points: from the centre the arc is seen at a larger angle.

    Step 1 · Concept

    2 · Angles, triangles, the circle #

    • Adjacent angles share a side, and the other two sides form a straight line: together 180°. Vertically opposite angles are equal.
    • A TransversalA line that crosses two other lines and forms pairs of angles with them.To the glossary crosses two lines and forms pairs of angles: corresponding, alternate, co-interior.
    • Similar trianglesTriangles of the same shape: the angles are equal, the sides are proportional.To the glossary have the same shape: the angles are equal, the sides are proportional.
    • A central angle has its vertex at the centre of a circle, an Inscribed angleAn angle with its vertex on a circle whose sides cut the circle.To the glossary one on the circle. A tangent has one common point with the circle.
    • A Property and testThe two directions of a theorem: what follows from the kind of figure, and how to recognise that kind.To the glossary says what follows from a figure being of a certain kind; a test says how to recognise that kind. These are two directions of one theorem, and they are not always both true.
    Step 2 · Law

    3 · Laws of figures #

    Parallel lines and a transversal

    Lines are parallel if and only if the corresponding angles are equal; the alternate angles are then equal too, and the co-interior angles add up to 180°.

    Corollary of the law «Parallel lines and a transversal»

    Angles of a parallelogram

    ∠A+∠B=180∘,∠A=∠C,∠B=∠D\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ,\qquad \angle A = \angle C,\quad \angle B = \angle D

    Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180°, opposite angles are equal.

    Figure 36. Corollary: adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180°, opposite angles are equal.

    Why it is so. The sides AD and BC are parallel, AB is a transversal, so the angles A and B are co-interior: A + B = 180°. In the same way B + C = 180° for the parallel AB and CD, hence A = C. So a parallelogram with angles x and 2x exists: x + 2x = 180°, the angles are 60° and 120°.

    The angle sum of a triangle is 180°

    ∠A+∠B+∠C=180∘,Sn=180∘(n−2)\angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ,\qquad S_n = 180^\circ (n - 2)

    Inscribed angle

    An inscribed angle equals half the central angle that stands on the same arc. An inscribed angle that stands on a diameter is a right angle.

    Corollary of the law «Inscribed angle»

    Inscribed quadrilateral

    ∠A+∠C=∠B+∠D=180∘\angle A + \angle C = \angle B + \angle D = 180^\circ

    If a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, its opposite angles add up to 180°. A circle can be drawn around a trapezium only when it is isosceles (an isosceles trapezium, US: isosceles trapezoid).

    Figure 37. Corollary: in an inscribed quadrilateral, opposite angles add up to 180°.

    Why it is so. The angles A and C stand on two arcs that together make the whole circle, 360°. Each inscribed angle is half its arc, so A + C = 360° : 2 = 180°. In a trapezium ABCD with bases AD and BC the angles A and B are co-interior: A + B = 180°; in an inscribed one also B + D = 180°, so A = D, and the trapezium is isosceles.

    Corollary of the law «Inscribed angle»

    Centre of the circumscribed circle

    The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle meet at one point, the Circumcentre (US: circumcenter)The point equidistant from all the vertices of a triangle: where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.To the glossary . In a right triangle it is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, in an obtuse one a point outside the triangle.

    Figure 38. Corollary: the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle meet at the centre of the circumscribed circle.

    Why it is so. Each point of the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B: two right triangles with a common leg and equal second legs have equal hypotenuses (Pythagoras' theorem, block 11). The point where two bisectors meet is equidistant from all three vertices - it is the centre of the circle. A right angle stands on a diameter, so in a right triangle the hypotenuse is a diameter and the centre is its midpoint. An obtuse angle C is half of the arc AB larger than a semicircle, so C and the centre lie on different sides of AB.

    Triangle inequality

    a<b+c,b<a+c,c<a+ba < b + c,\quad b < a + c,\quad c < a + b

    It is enough to check that the largest side is less than the sum of the other two.

    Similarity test by two angles

    If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar.

    Corollary of the law «Similarity test by two angles»

    MidlineThe segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle or of the legs of a trapezium (US: trapezoid).To the glossary of a triangle and of a trapezium

    MN∥AC,MN=AC2;mtrap=a+b2MN \parallel AC,\quad MN = \frac{AC}{2};\qquad m_{\text{trap}} = \frac{a + b}{2}

    The midline joins the midpoints of two sides of a triangle: it is parallel to the third side and equals half of it. The midline of a trapezium joins the midpoints of the legs, is parallel to the bases and equals half their sum.

    Figure 39. Corollary: the midline of a triangle is parallel to the third side and equals half of it.

    Why it is so. Through the midpoint M of the side AB draw a line parallel to AC; it meets BC at the point N. Corresponding angles at parallel lines are equal, so the triangles MBN and ABC are similar by two angles with ratio BM : BA = 1 : 2. Hence BN = BC/2, that is, N is the midpoint, and MN = AC/2. A diagonal divides a trapezium into two triangles, and the midline of the trapezium is made of the midlines of these triangles: a/2 + b/2.

    Step 3 · Why it is so

    4 · Where the laws come from #

    The angle sum of a triangle. Draw through the vertex B a line parallel to AC. The angles at B formed by it are alternate with the angles A and C, so they are equal to them. The three angles at B together form a straight angle: 180°. Here you see what the theorem stands on: the property of parallel lines.

    Figure 40. The angle sum of a triangle: the three angles at vertex B make a straight line.

    A polygon. The diagonals from one vertex divide a convex n-gon into n−2n - 2 triangles, and the angles of the triangles together make up the angles of the polygon.

    The inscribed angle. Let one side of an inscribed angle pass through the centre O. The triangle with vertices at O, at the vertex of the angle and on the circle is isosceles (two sides are radii), and the central angle is its exterior angle, that is, the sum of two equal angles. So the inscribed angle is half the central one. Other positions reduce to this one.

    Figure 41. An inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc: 100° and 50°.

    The triangle inequality. A segment is the shortest path between two points, so the path through the third vertex is longer.

    Step 4 · Limits

    5 · Where the laws break #

    A figure is not an argument. Angles that «look equal» are equal only when this follows from the condition and the theorems.

    A property does not always reverse. The diagonals of a rectangle are equal, but an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals too. In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, but they are equal only in a rectangle.

    The triangle inequality is strict. If c=a+bc = a + b, the three points lie on one line, and there is no triangle.

    Step 5 · Practice

    6 · Tasks in the NMT format #

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find the largest angle.

    Laws: the angle sum and the part of a whole from block 2.

    There are 9 parts in all, one part is 180∘:9=20∘180^\circ : 9 = 20^\circ, the largest angle is 4·20∘=80∘4 \cdot 20^\circ = 80^\circ.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Find the angle sum of a convex hexagon (in degrees).

    Law: the angle sum of a polygon.

    180∘·(6−2)=720∘180^\circ \cdot (6 - 2) = 720^\circ: four triangles.

    Short answer · 2 points

    A central angle of a circle is 110°. Find the inscribed angle (in degrees) that stands on the same arc.

    Law: inscribed angle.

    Half the central one: 55°.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Which triple of segments can form a triangle?

    Law: the triangle inequality.

    Only 5<3+45 < 3 + 4. In A and D the largest side equals the sum of the other two: this is the limit, the triangle degenerates into a segment.

    Short answer · 2 points

    The sides of a triangle are 8 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. Find the perimeter of the triangle whose vertices are the midpoints of the sides of the given one (in cm).

    Figure 42. For the task: a triangle whose vertices are the midpoints of the sides of triangle ABC.

    Corollary: the midline of a triangle.

    Each side of the new triangle is a midline, that is, half a side of the given one: (8 + 10 + 12) : 2 = 15.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    In triangle ABC ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 70°. Find the exterior angle of the triangle at the vertex C.

    Figure 43. For the task: the exterior angle of a triangle at vertex C.

    Law: the angle sum of a triangle.

    ∠C = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°, the exterior angle is 180° − 60° = 120°: it is the sum of the two angles not adjacent to it. 60° is the angle C itself, 110° and 130° are the exterior angles at B and A.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    AB is a diameter of a circle, the point C lies on the circle, ∠ABC = 35°. Find ∠BAC.

    Figure 44. For the task: a triangle inscribed in a circle, one side of which is a diameter.

    Law: inscribed angle: an angle that stands on a diameter is a right angle.

    ∠ACB stands on a semicircle, so it equals 180° : 2 = 90°, and ∠BAC = 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°. 145° is 180° − 35°, as if there were no angle C.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Data on the figure · read and apply. The numbers for the solution are only on the figure: first write them down, then solve.

    Find the angle C of the triangle ABC shown in the figure (in degrees).

    Figure 45. For the task: a triangle with two marked angles.

    Law: the angle sum of a triangle.

    From the figure: ∠A = 48°, ∠B = 67°. ∠C = 180° − 48° − 67° = 65°.

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Data on the figure · pick what is needed. The numbers are only on the figure, and among them is an extra one or a trap: the grid step, a scale that does not start at zero. Write down only what the solution needs.

    Find the angle B of the parallelogram ABCD shown in the figure.

    Figure 46. For the task: a parallelogram with a marked angle and a labelled side.

    Corollary: angles of a parallelogram.

    Only the angle A = 58° is needed: adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180°, so ∠B = 180° − 58° = 122°. The side length 7 cm is not needed for the angles. 58° is the angle C, opposite A.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Data on the figure · read and connect. The numbers are only on the figure, and what you read goes into two laws: write the numbers down, then name both laws.

    Find the angle ABC of the triangle shown in the figure (in degrees).

    Figure 47. For the task: an inscribed triangle, a central angle and an inscribed angle.

    Laws: inscribed angle and the angle sum of a triangle.

    From the figure: the central angle AOB = 130°, ∠CAB = 70°. The inscribed angle ACB stands on the same arc AB, so it is half as large: 65°. Then ∠ABC = 180° − 65° − 70° = 45°.
    Step 6 · Reverse move

    7 · Name the law yourself #

    Short answer · 2 points

    Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the co-interior angles is 65°. Find the other (in degrees).

    Law: parallel lines and a transversal.

    180∘−65∘=115∘180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ.

    Short answer · 2 points

    The point C lies on a circle with diameter AB, ∠A=35∘\angle A = 35^\circ. Find the angle B of the triangle ABC (in degrees).

    Laws: an inscribed angle on a diameter and the angle sum.

    The angle C stands on a diameter, so ∠C=90∘\angle C = 90^\circ; then ∠B=180∘−90∘−35∘=55∘\angle B = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ.

    8 · Find the mistake in someone else's solution #

    Viktoria writes: «The diagonals of the quadrilateral ABCD are equal, so ABCD is a rectangle».

    Where is the mistake?

    Equal diagonals are a property of a rectangle but not a test: an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals too, and even a quadrilateral with no parallel sides at all. The test for a rectangle: a parallelogram with equal diagonals (the second limit).

    What you have after this page #

    A chain instead of a list. Parallel lines give the angle sum of a triangle, the angle sum of a triangle gives the angle sum of a polygon, an isosceles triangle of radii gives the inscribed angle. If you forget a fact, you can rebuild it from the previous one.

    Frequency on this site, not in the NMT: this page has 12 trainer tasks, and they lean on these laws: The angle sum of a triangle is 180° - 6, Inscribed angle - 4, Parallel lines and a transversal - 2, Similarity test by two angles - 1, Triangle inequality - 1. In real NMT papers of 2024-2026 this block is needed in 15 tasks out of 132: Similarity test by two angles - 5, The angle sum of a triangle is 180° - 4, Inscribed angle - 3, Angles, triangles, the circle - 2, Parallel lines and a transversal - 2, Triangle inequality - 2.

    You know this block if you:

    1. solve 8 tasks out of 10 on angles, triangles and the circle without a hint;
    2. can explain aloud why the angle sum of a triangle is 180°;
    3. find the mistake in someone else's solution, as in Viktoria's.
